promptText: Why does calling a hook conditionally (e.g. inside an `if` block) break React, given that the runtime doesn't check hook names at all?
options: React identifies each hook call by its position in a fixed call order — an internal linked list of 'slots' per component. Skipping a hook on some renders shifts every subsequent hook to the wrong slot, so React returns the wrong state for them
Conditional hooks cause a JavaScript syntax error at parse time
React only allows a maximum of one conditional statement per component
Hooks are identified by variable name, so conditional calls just rename the slot
explanation: React has no concept of hook names — it tracks hooks purely by the order they're called in, storing each one in a slot in an ordered linked list on the fiber. If a hook is skipped on some render, every hook after it shifts by one position, causing React to hand back state that belongs to a different hook entirely.

promptText: Why does calling `setCount(count + 1)` three times in a row inside one event handler only increment the counter by 1, while `setCount(c => c + 1)` three times increments it by 3?
options: React batches multiple identical-looking calls into one automatically for performance, regardless of form

`count` in `count + 1` is a snapshot value captured from the current render's closure — all three calls read the same stale value; the functional updater form `c => c + 1` instead queues each update against the latest pending value, so each one actually builds on the last
setCount can only be called once per event handler; the extra calls are silently ignored
count + 1 causes a type coercion bug that makes the value stick at 1
explanation: State setters don't mutate a live variable — `count` in the handler's scope is a fixed value from that render. Calling setCount(count + 1) three times just computes the same result three times; the updater function form receives the actual latest queued value each time it runs, correctly compounding the updates.

promptText: What is the core timing difference between `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect`?
options: useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser paints; useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after the DOM is updated but before the browser paints
useLayoutEffect only runs once per component's entire lifetime, regardless of dependencies
useEffect can only be used for data fetching; useLayoutEffect can only be used for DOM measurement
They run at the exact same time; the only difference is naming convention
explanation: Both share the same API and dependency semantics, but useEffect is deferred until after the browser has painted (non-blocking), while useLayoutEffect runs synchronously right after DOM mutations and before paint, blocking the visual update until it completes.

promptText: What is the precise relationship between `useCallback(fn, deps)` and `useMemo`?
options: useCallback(fn, deps) is functionally equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)` — it caches a function reference, while useMemo more generally caches the result of any computation
useCallback is deprecated in favor of useMemo and should never be used in new code
useMemo can only cache primitive values; useCallback can only cache functions
They are unrelated APIs that happen to share a similar dependency-array signature
explanation: useCallback is literally defined as a convenience wrapper: useCallback(fn, deps) caches the function fn itself the same way useMemo(() => fn, deps) would cache it as the memoized 'computed value' — the only difference is what's being memoized, a function versus an arbitrary result.

promptText: If two different components both call the same custom hook `useToggle()`, do they share the same toggle state?
options: Yes, custom hooks always share a single global state instance across all callers
No — each component that calls the hook gets its own independent, isolated instance of that hook's internal state; only the logic/behavior is shared, not the data itself
It depends on whether the hook uses useState or useReducer internally
They share state only if both components are rendered inside the same parent
explanation: A custom hook is just a function that happens to call other hooks — every call site gets a completely separate copy of whatever state those inner hooks create. Sharing actual state across components requires something else, like Context or an external store, not a plain custom hook.

promptText: Why is `useRef` unsuitable for storing a value that the rendered UI needs to visually reflect, like a counter shown on screen?
options: useRef values are reset to their initial value on every render

Mutating a ref's .current is intentionally invisible to React's render cycle — it never schedules a re-render, so the screen simply won't update to show the new value even though the ref's internal value did change
Refs can only store DOM nodes, never plain numbers or objects
Refs throw an error if read outside of a useEffect
explanation: useRef is explicitly designed so that writing to .current does not cause a re-render — it's meant for bookkeeping the render doesn't need to reflect (timers, DOM nodes, previous values). Anything that should visibly update on screen must be state (useState/useReducer), not a ref.

promptText: `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => console.log(count), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, []);` always logs 0, no matter how many times `count` has actually changed. What is happening, and what is the best fix for a counter?
options: setInterval has a bug that prevents it from reading updated variables; the fix is to use setTimeout in a recursive loop instead

The effect's closure captured `count` from the initial render (since deps are []) and that captured value never updates; the best fix here is to use the functional updater form inside the interval, e.g. `setCount(c => c + 1)`, which never needs to read the stale captured value at all
The fix is to remove the cleanup function so the interval never gets cleared
This is expected correct behavior; count is not supposed to update inside a setInterval
explanation: Because the effect only runs once (empty deps), the interval's callback closes over the count value from that one render forever — a classic stale closure. Since the bug here is really about reading (not needing) the current value, switching to the functional updater form for updates sidesteps the stale read entirely, without needing to re-subscribe the interval on every count change.

promptText: `const filters = { status: "open" }; useEffect(() => { fetchTasks(filters); }, [filters]);` causes the effect to run on every single render, hammering the API. What is the root cause?
options: fetchTasks is inherently asynchronous and always triggers a fresh render

`filters` is a fresh object literal created on every render, so even though its contents look identical, its reference is different each time — Object.is sees a 'changed' dependency every render, re-running the effect endlessly
useEffect requires exactly one dependency; using an object instead of a primitive is invalid syntax
fetchTasks itself must be missing from the dependency array, which is the actual cause
explanation: Object/array/function literals created directly in the component body are brand-new references every render. Even though `{ status: "open" }` looks the same each time, Object.is (the comparison useEffect uses) sees it as a different value, so the dependency 'changes' on every render — the fix is to depend on the primitive fields (like filters.status) or wrap the object in useMemo.

promptText: A context Provider supplies `value={{ user, theme, setTheme }}` as a fresh object literal on every render. What happens to every component that calls `useContext` on this context whenever ANY of those fields changes, including ones a given consumer never reads?
options: Only components that read the specific field that changed re-render; React tracks field-level dependencies automatically
Every consumer of that context re-renders, regardless of which specific field it actually reads — Context re-renders are all-or-nothing per context object, with no built-in field-level subscription
No components re-render, since the value's structure is unchanged
Only class components subscribed via contextType re-render; function components using useContext are unaffected
explanation: React only compares the entire context value by reference; when it changes (here, on every render because a fresh object is created each time), every consumer re-renders regardless of whether the specific field it reads actually changed — this all-or-nothing behavior is why splitting contexts or memoizing the value matters.

promptText: What is the actual criterion for choosing `useReducer` over `useState`, rather than just 'the state is large'?
options: useReducer should be used whenever there are more than three pieces of state, regardless of how they relate to each other

The right signal is HOW state changes — useReducer is worth it when several related values update together in response to one event, or when update logic follows clear 'action' semantics that benefit from being centralized in one pure function, not merely the size of the state
useReducer is required for any state used inside a useEffect
useState cannot hold object values, only primitives, so useReducer is needed for objects
explanation: The deciding factor is the shape of the state transitions, not raw size — a single boolean toggled through many coordinated paths can justify a reducer, while three genuinely independent primitive values usually don't, even though the second case has more total state.

promptText: A component does `const [fullName, setFullName] = useState(""); useEffect(() => { setFullName(first + " " + last); }, [first, last]);` to keep a derived value in sync. What is the recommended fix, and why?
options: Add fullName itself to the effect's dependency array to make the sync more reliable

Compute `const fullName = first + " " + last;` directly during render instead of syncing it via an effect — this removes an entire redundant state variable, an extra render cycle, and a possible one-frame window of stale data
Wrap the effect in useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect
This pattern is already correct and is the idiomatic way to derive state in React
explanation: Storing derived data in its own state and syncing it with an effect creates a redundant source of truth and an unnecessary extra render; anything computable from existing props/state should simply be computed inline during render (memoized only if genuinely expensive), not stored and synchronized separately.

promptText: Why does `useEffect(async () => { await fetch(url); }, [id])` produce a React warning, and what's the correct way to do async work in an effect?
options: useEffect callbacks must return either undefined or a cleanup function; an async function always returns a Promise, which React can't interpret as a valid cleanup — the fix is to define an inner async function inside the effect and call it, keeping the effect's own callback synchronous
async functions cannot be called from inside any React hook under any circumstances
The warning is purely cosmetic and can be safely ignored with no functional consequence
fetch() is not allowed inside useEffect at all; it must be called in an event handler instead
explanation: An async function's implicit return value is always a Promise, and useEffect expects its callback to return nothing or a synchronous cleanup function — passing an async function directly breaks that contract. The standard fix defines and immediately invokes an inner async function, letting the outer effect callback stay synchronous and optionally return a real cleanup function.

promptText: A developer explains: 'I wrapped the expensive filter operation in startTransition so it runs in the background on another thread, keeping the UI responsive.' What is factually wrong with this explanation, and what does startTransition actually do?
options: Nothing is wrong; startTransition genuinely dispatches the work to a background thread via the browser's scheduler

React's concurrent scheduler is still single-threaded and cooperative — startTransition doesn't move work off the main JS thread or parallelize anything; it only lets React deprioritize and interrupt that specific render relative to more urgent updates (like the next keystroke), yielding back to the browser between chunks of work on the same thread
startTransition only works when combined with a Web Worker, so the explanation is correct as long as a worker is also used
startTransition pauses all other rendering in the app until the transition completes
explanation: This is one of the most common misconceptions about React's concurrent features: transitions change scheduling priority and allow interruption/restart of in-progress render work, but everything still executes on the same single main thread — genuinely offloading heavy computation requires an actual Web Worker, which is an entirely separate mechanism.

promptText: A custom `getSnapshot` function is implemented as `() => ({ ...store.state })`, returning a fresh object every call. What bug does this cause with `useSyncExternalStore`, and why?
options: This is the correct, recommended implementation and causes no issues

Because getSnapshot creates a brand-new object reference on every single call, `Object.is` comparison between successive snapshots never matches, so React concludes the store changed on every check — producing continuous, infinite re-renders. The fix is to return a cached, stable reference that's only rebuilt when the store's own state actually changes
getSnapshot is only allowed to run once, at mount, so this has no runtime effect at all
This bug only occurs in React's development build and not in production
explanation: useSyncExternalStore compares successive getSnapshot() results with Object.is to decide whether to re-render; a getSnapshot that spreads/rebuilds a new object every call will never produce two equal references, causing React to think the store changed every time it checks — the fix is to cache the derived snapshot and only replace the cached reference when the underlying data genuinely changes.

promptText: A reducer case does `case "ADD_ITEM": state.items.push(action.item); return state;` — dispatching this action doesn't cause the component to re-render, even though the items array visibly gained an element. Why does this specific bug occur, connecting reducer behavior to React's general re-render mechanism?
options: push() throws an exception inside reducers, which React silently swallows

React bails out of re-rendering when a reducer's returned state is Object.is-equal to the previous state — the same optimization useState relies on. Since the case mutates `state.items` in place and returns the exact same `state` object reference, React sees 'no change' at the top level even though the array's actual contents changed
useReducer does not support array-based state at all
dispatch() only re-renders the component every third call due to internal batching
explanation: Just like useState, useReducer bails out of re-rendering when the reducer's return value is reference-equal (Object.is) to the previous state. Mutating state.items in place and returning the same top-level state object means React's shallow reference check sees no change, so it skips the re-render entirely — the fix is always to return a new object/array reference, e.g. `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }`.
